summary:
Carlos Alcaraz was ahead, and then suddenly he was not. In the second set of his Japan Open match, the Spanish tennis player led Alex Michelsen 4–2. Michelsen won the next four games and took the set 6–4.

Alcaraz had already won the first set in a tiebreak. With one set each, the match now needed a deciding set. Alcaraz won that final set 6–1 and took the first-round match. The full score was 7–6(1), 4–6, 6–1.

The event’s report describes two challenges. Michelsen’s powerful shots and quick movement troubled Alcaraz. The court conditions also felt different from the indoor court where Alcaraz had practised after arriving in Tokyo.

Alcaraz said he needed to change how he was playing. As the match continued, his shots became more precise. He accepted the conditions and found his own game again.

He did not say everything had gone perfectly. Instead, he was pleased to win a difficult opening match in three sets.

The exciting part is how the story changed. A lead disappeared, the opponent levelled the match, and Alcaraz still had a final set in which to respond. The result came after an adjustment, rather than an easy march from start to finish.
title: Alcaraz Changes His Game After Losing a Lead
why_it_matters: The match gives a concrete example of changing an approach after a setback.
